title: Severance Wells: Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Severance wells have a 30 ft median depth, 20 gpm median yield, and estimated finished costs of $7,000-$13,600.
h1: Severance, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Severance sits on the plains, and the nearby permit records show generally shallow wells. Among wells with reported depths, the median is 30 feet, with the middle half between 22 and 39 feet. Reported yields are also strong overall, but the records are uneven: 1,751 permits are on file, while 1,078 report a total depth and only 191 report a pump yield.

That makes the map useful for setting expectations, not for guaranteeing a particular lot. Ground conditions, the intended use, casing and grout requirements, pump equipment, and the location of the well on the property still affect the final result. Check nearby permits before buying land near Windsor, Timnath, Eaton, Greeley, Ault, or Pierce.

sections.heading: How deep are wells around Severance?
sections.html:
Severance-area wells are usually shallow. The reported depth median is 30 feet, and the middle half runs from 22 to 39 feet. Ninety-two percent of reported wells are under 100 feet. Only 2% fall between 100 and 300 feet, 4% between 300 and 600 feet, and 2% are deeper than 600 feet.

The deepest record is 3,340 feet, so an occasional outlier exists. Most local drilling bids should be based on shallow alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, but a driller still needs to evaluate the specific lot. For a buyer, the 30-foot median is a useful starting point for comparing bids, not a promised completion depth. A neighboring well can be a better guide than a countywide assumption.

sections.heading: What water yield can Severance wells produce?
sections.html:
The median reported pump yield is 20.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 13.0 to 200.0 gallons per minute. Seventy percent of reported wells produce more than 15 gallons per minute. Another 23% fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, 7% between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, and 1% under 1 gallon per minute.

Those figures describe reported tests, not a guarantee for an un drilled well. Only 191 wells report a pump yield, so the sample is smaller than the permit total. A result under 1 gallon per minute would be a serious buyer concern, while a stronger well can provide more operating margin for household use. Ask for the neighboring well’s permit, yield test, pump information, and intended use.

sections.heading: Is the water table changing near Severance?
sections.html:
Reported static water levels are shallow. The median depth to water is 11 feet, and the middle half is 8 to 18 feet below the surface. That matters during drilling, excavation, septic planning, and construction because shallow groundwater can affect access, trenching, and site drainage.

The decade comparison does not show a clear large decline in this record: the median static level was 9 feet below the surface in the 2010s and 10 feet in the 2020s. That is a one-foot difference in the reported medians, not proof that water levels are stable on every parcel. Static levels can vary by season, pumping, and local conditions. Have the driller verify conditions at the proposed well location.

sections.heading: Who has drilled near Severance, and when?
sections.html:
Permit activity extends across many decades, with the newest permit year in 2025. The records include 73 permits from the 1950s, 124 from the 1960s, 162 from the 1970s, 122 from the 1980s, 200 from the 1990s, 339 from the 2000s, 170 from the 2010s, and 191 from the 2020s.

The most active names in these records are Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 314 wells; Lesh Drilling Inc. (Lesh Jr., Ed), with 227; and R & R Well & Pump Inc. (Rank, Samuel C), with 74. These are permit-record counts, not a recommendation or a current availability list. Confirm licensing, insurance, scheduling, scope, and references before hiring.

sections.heading: What does a new well cost in Severance?
sections.html:
For the local ground conditions, the drilling model uses a typical rate of $35 to $55 per foot. At the 30-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $1,000 to $1,600. That is only the hole. A finished well, including the pump, tank, trenching, and electrical, is estimated at $7,000 to $13,600.

A bid can move outside that range if the site needs unusual casing or grout work, a longer water line, difficult equipment access, or different pumping equipment. Ask the contractor to separate drilling, casing, grout, development, pump and tank, trenching, electrical, testing, and permit-related work. Comparing a complete scope is more useful than comparing only the per-foot rate.

sections.heading: What risks should a Severance buyer check?
sections.html:
Permit records name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer for 1,411 wells, Alluvial for 118, and Quaternary Alluvium for 41. They name no Denver Basin aquifer wells in this area. Fractured ground can be unpredictable, while shallow alluvial conditions can make water quality and seasonal groundwater important questions.

There are 726 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 2 historic mine features, and 4 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites mapped within about 10 miles. These locations do not prove contamination at a particular lot. Test the existing well water for relevant contaminants and confirm treatment needs. Also check septic setbacks, building envelopes, access for a rig, drainage, and whether the intended household, stock, or irrigation use matches the permit.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a Severance lot
sections.html:
Start with the DWR permit and construction record for the property, then compare wells nearby in Severance and the surrounding areas. Look for reported depth, static water level, yield, construction details, and use. The local records include domestic or household, stock, irrigation, and monitoring wells, so not every nearby permit represents a home water supply.

A new household well generally needs the correct DWR permit, and an exempt household-use well still has limits, including the 35 gallon-per-minute pumping limit. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be required for some uses. Before closing, make the well and water-quality review part of the inspection period. Before building, coordinate the well location with septic, driveway access, utility trenches, drainage, and the planned home.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Severance, Colorado?
faq.a: The reported median well depth near Severance is 30 feet, and the middle half runs from 22 to 39 feet. Ninety-two percent of reported wells are under 100 feet. The record also includes a 3,340-foot well, so unusual conditions occur. Use nearby permits and a driller’s site review to estimate a specific property’s depth.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Severance?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $35 to $55 per foot. At the 30-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $1,000 to $1,600. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $7,000 to $13,600. Get a written scope because equipment, access, casing, grout, and trench length affect the total.

faq.q: How much water does a Severance well produce?
faq.a: Reported yields have a 20.0 gallon-per-minute median, with the middle half from 13.0 to 200.0 gallons per minute. Seventy percent report more than 15 gallons per minute, while 1% report under 1 gallon per minute. Only 191 wells report a pump yield, so these figures are a guide, not a guarantee for a new well.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Severance?
faq.a: The permit map cannot establish that a particular well is safe to drink. Within about 10 miles, 726 PFAS sampling or contamination sites are mapped, along with 4 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test an existing well before relying on it, and ask a qualified laboratory about PFAS and other tests appropriate to the property’s location and well construction.

faq.q: Should I check a well permit before buying near Severance?
faq.a: Yes. The area has 1,751 DWR permits, but only 1,078 report total depth, 191 report pump yield, and 108 report static water level. Review the property’s permit and compare nearby records for depth, yield, water level, construction, and use. Also confirm the proposed household use is allowed and check septic, access, drainage, and building constraints.
